targetSkill: Teach the student to recover meaning from sentences whose syntactic structure — long clauses, embedded phrases, inverted order, parenthetical interruptions, multiple modifiers, archaic constructions — creates a parsing barrier. The student is not analyzing craft; the student is learning to deconstruct complex sentences into their core grammatical units (subject, verb, object, modifier) so meaning becomes accessible.
mustHave: A passage with at least one sentence whose syntactic complexity creates a real parsing challenge — long sentence (30+ words), embedded clauses, inversion, interruption by parenthetical phrases, or chains of modifiers before the main verb
Complexity that is syntactic, not vocabulary-based — a student who knows every word in the sentence still has to work to identify who did what to whom
A core meaning that IS recoverable once the sentence is deconstructed — the syntax hides the meaning but does not obliterate it
Sentence structure that rewards teaching — once a student identifies the subject, verb, and core predicate, the rest of the sentence resolves into clear modification
mustNotHave: Passages where complexity is primarily lexical (unfamiliar vocabulary) rather than syntactic — that's vocabulary_gap, not syntax_barrier
Passages where the complex sentence has no recoverable core — syntax so tangled that no amount of parsing produces a clear subject-verb-object
Short or simple sentences that lack genuine syntactic barriers — student gets no practice if the sentence is trivial to parse

Passages where the parsing barrier requires specific historical, political, religious, or cultural knowledge a 9th grader is unlikely to have (e.g., archaic legal or biblical constructions requiring schema)
Paragraphs dominated by dialogue (60%+ quotation marks) — dialogue syntax is conversational, not the authorial syntactic challenge this primitive targets
Nonfiction biographical or memoir prose about real people's lives; syntax practice requires authorial fiction where sentence construction is deliberate
Extremely archaic prose whose syntax is so foreign to modern English that parsing practice would not transfer (Middle English, heavily Latinate 17th-century prose)
Poetry where the syntactic inversion is metrical rather than rhetorical

tierSignals.tier1: One moderately long sentence (30-50 words) with one embedded clause or one inversion. Once the student identifies the subject and main verb, the rest falls into place. Parsing practice is focused and bounded.
tierSignals.tier2: A sentence with two or three embedded structures — a relative clause AND a parenthetical interruption, or a long introductory phrase AND inversion. Student must deconstruct in steps: find the core, then unpack the modifiers.
tierSignals.tier3: A sentence with multiple nested structures — clauses within clauses, modifiers stacked before the main verb, delayed subject or verb across 40+ words. Student must hold the sentence in mind and patiently resolve it. Requires re-reading with a parsing strategy.
